transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-06-17 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m
Attendees: Jamie Ford (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Lucia Gomez (Redwood Solutions); Liam Chen (Quantaco Head of ML), Sofia Martinez (Quantaco Infra), Avery Brooks (Quantaco Product), Noah Patel (Quantaco SRE)

[00:00] Jamie: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is the weekly sync for the POC, focusing on cost economics this week. quick roll call?
[00:08] Liam: hey yep liam here, sofia, avery and noah also on our side
[00:12] Jamie: awesome, priya and lucia with me from redwood
[00:15] Priya: hi all
[00:18] [00:22] Jamie: quick agenda, we will go over the updated cost spreadsheet i sent this morning, talk through the caching numbers from our side, batching tradeoffs and the quantization experiments, then align on the final benchmark to run this week and next steps
[00:36] Liam: sounds good
[00:38] [00:40] Jamie: ok priya do you want to kick off with the tokens per dollar summary?
[00:43] Priya: yeah sure, so high-level, we recalculated tokens per dollar for your workload traces you shared — the core lens is tokens/sec per dollar, which we compute by combining measured tokens/sec on a given instance type and the instance cost/hour (we included both hosted and dedicated pricing scenarios). for your median chat length the gpt-sized open models we tested yield roughly 12k-18k tokens per second at p99 latency around 350-450ms when running on our c4-like dedicated profile with q4f16 quant. cost per million tokens is about $0.60 in hosted, and with dedicated reserved capacity that drops to roughly $0.18 to $0.25 depending on commit and packing.
[01:32] Sofia: sorry can i interrupt — when you say tokens/sec per dollar are you normalizing across batching? like what's the baseline batch we used?
[01:38] Priya: good q — baseline was continuous batching with effective batch size around 8 for the traces you shared; we also ran controlled tests at batch sizes 1, 4, 8, 16 to show tradeoffs
[01:47] [01:50] Priya: at batch=1 latency is low but throughput is poor; batch 8 tends to be the sweet spot for your average request distribution — it gives near-linear throughput increases while p99 still holds under our SLO. batch 16 improves tokens/sec by ~30% but p99 jumps by ~60-80ms for long context cases.
[02:10] Avery: and that 30% delta is tokens/sec or cost?
[02:12] Priya: tokens/sec; cost per token falls accordingly since you're amortizing fixed kernel overheads, so tokens per dollar improves ~25-30% moving 8->16 depending on model and quant. but important caveat, if you have strict p99 latency SLOs for interactive flows, batch 16 may violate that in tail cases.
[02:35] [02:38] Jamie: exactly — so it's a tradeoff: if product needs snappy interactive replies you keep smaller batch sizes and rely more on caching. if throughput/cost is primary then larger batches and dedicated capacity win.
[02:49] Liam: what about prefix caching? your last note said big savings with KV-cache for sessions?
[02:53] Priya: yes — we simulated prefix/KV caching with your session traces. when we enable short-term prefix cache (we cached the first N tokens and the KV pairs for repeated prompts) for customer support flows where users ask follow-ups, we see up to 45% reduction in tokens sent to the model and around 2.2x improvement in tokens/sec served from cache hits because you avoid recomputing the whole context. overall cost per conversation dropped ~35% in our sim.
[03:26] Sofia: is that sensitive to TTLs? like how long you keep cache entries?
[03:29] Priya: yes TTL choice matters — we recommended default TTL of 10 minutes for support workflows based on your inter-message gap distributions; longer TTLs help but increase cache memory footprint and potential staleness concerns. lucia can add recommended settings to a runbook.
[03:44] Lucia: yep i'll draft the runbook with recommended TTLs, eviction policy and keys to watch.
[03:48] [03:50] Noah: curious on storage/ops costs — does the KV-cache add significant infra costs?
[03:54] Priya: it's modest; for your 50k concurrent sessions estimate the cache footprint is in the low hundreds of GBs, hosted-managed cache adds a small monthly cost which is more than offset by tokens savings; we'll break that out in the spreadsheet.
[04:11] [04:12] Jamie: moving on to quantization and throughput — we ran q4f16, q5_0 and int8-like profiles. q4f16 is a good cost-performance mix for your models; q5 gave extra throughput but at small quality regressions on longer completions in our evals.
[04:29] Priya: int8 provided the best tokens/sec but needed extra recomputation for certain operators which increased tail latency unexpectedly in some cases; so int8 is best for pure batch inference workloads rather than interactive chat.
[04:42] Liam: what's the plan if we need to mix interactive and batch? do we spin different pools?
[04:46] Priya: yes we recommended heterogeneous pools — small low-latency pool for interactive (smaller batches, q4f16), and separate high-throughput pool for batched background jobs (larger batches, int8 or q5). the smart routing layer can route by policy and fallback to compatible variants if needed.
[05:03] [05:05] Avery: any surprises in the profiling?
[05:07] Priya: one thing — your long-context reranker path has lots of repeated prefix tokens which makes it an excellent candidate for prefix caching; also we saw a small kernel-level bottleneck at sequence length ~2.5k on a particular kernel combo, so we suggested slightly different kernel selection in those ranges which improved tokens/sec by ~8%.
[05:25] [05:30] Jamie: ok let's talk numbers in the spreadsheet — i pulled up the shared sheet (referenced in the calendar) and walked through the hosted vs dedicated columns
[05:36] Jamie: hosted cost per million tokens $0.60, dedicated effective cost ranges $0.18-$0.25 depending on commit and shared packing. with caching enabled the effective cost could drop to ~$0.12-$0.14 per million for your median workloads.
[05:53] Liam: that delta to $0.12 seems optimistic — what's driving that?
[05:56] Priya: two levers — 1) caching reduces model input tokens substantially for follow-up heavy sessions, 2) higher packing efficiency on dedicated GPUs and ability to run larger batches for background jobs. both together compound.
[06:12] [06:15] Sofia: for the dedicated scenario, what's the recommended commit size? you mentioned reserved capacity tiers?
[06:20] Jamie: we modeled three commit tiers — small (1-2 cards), medium (4-8), and large (16+). your projected steady throughput maps to medium where you get best per-token economics without excessive upfront commit. we also modeled burst capacity pricing.
[06:33] [06:35] Noah: operationally what about autoscaling and SLOs — if we run dedicated and suddenly spike, will fallback to hosted add cost unpredictably?
[06:42] Priya: fallback is policy driven — you can cap fallback usage or set hard fallbacks to avoid bill surprises; we suggest a safety buffer in the dedicated pool to cover typical spikes then allow limited fallback for true outliers. the spreadsheet includes a sensitivity table showing costs with 5%, 10%, 20% fallback usage.
[07:03] [07:05] Liam: can we see the sensitivity table again after the call?
[07:07] Jamie: yes we'll share and highlight the rows — action item for me.
[07:10] [07:12] Priya: quick note on metrics and observability — Redwood Console can show token-level cost, per-route latency and per-model dashboards; we've included sample dashboard screenshots in the deck.
[07:23] Avery: one question on compliance — if we bounce to hosted for fallback, are we exposing any data residency issues?
[07:29] Jamie: good point — you can restrict fallbacks by region and enforce no-hosted fallback for sensitive routes; private deployments or dedicated with VPC are more appropriate if strict residency needed.
[07:43] [07:45] Sofia: ok so next for us is to run the benchmark you suggested — what's the exact benchmark config?
[07:50] Priya: we propose three runs: 1) baseline (no cache, batch=8, q4f16), 2) cache-enabled (TTL 10m, same batch), 3) mixed heavy-batch (batch=16 or 32, int8-like quant for background flows). each run should be 30-60 minutes with your real request traces replayed; collect p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/sec, and cost estimates.
[08:17] Noah: we'll need the exact replay script and runbook so infra can kick it off — can you provide?
[08:21] Lucia: yes i'll attach the replay script and a short runbook with the commands to enable prefix cache and the config flags.
[08:26] [08:30] Priya: also we'll include a small script to compute tokens/sec per dollar from the logs so it's straightforward to compare across runs.
[08:37] [08:40] Liam: timeline wise, if we run this week we can target results early next week and decide final success criteria.
[08:46] Jamie: yep that was the plan — ci schedule target is tuesday 2026-06-22 for results and then deep-dive on wednesday if needed.
[08:55] [09:00] Avery: any open product questions?
[09:02] Liam: just one — latency budgets per route, can we set per-route routing policies to prefer low-latency pool?
[09:07] Jamie: yes per-route policies supported; you can pin routes to pools and set fallback policies and latency budgets in the console. we'll include a short example policy in the runbook.
[09:18] [09:20] Priya: quick note — we did a small quality check after q5 quant: for your summarization prompts the pass rate dropped ~3% which may or may not be acceptable depending on production tolerance; recommended you validate on your critical evals.
[09:35] Sofia: ok we'll run a small regression eval in parallel.
[09:38] [09:40] Jamie: perfect. any other blockers?
[09:43] Liam: nothing major, just we want the sensitivity table and the exact scripts.
[09:47] Jamie: will do.
[09:50] [09:52] Lucia: action items recap — i'll share runbook + replay script; priya will share tokens/sec script; jamie shares updated spreadsheet and sensitivity tables; sofia/noah run the benchmark and share results by 2026-06-22.
[10:05] Jamie: great, thanks everyone. we'll regroup after you have the benchmark results — probably wednesday 2026-06-23 for the deep-dive. thanks!
[10:12] Liam: thanks all
[10:14] End of recording

Notes on transcript: transcription contains occasional name mis-recognitions and filler tokens; speakers overlapped at a few points. The technical details reference KV/prefix cache, q4f16 and int8 quant profiles, batch sizes 1-32 and sensitivity tables for dedicated/hosted fallback percentages.
